measures.meaning: After at least 8 hours without food. A fasting level of 7.0 mmol/L or above indicates diabetes and, without symptoms, is confirmed by a second test on another day. Normal fasting values differ slightly between countries and laboratories, so the report gives the range used.
Any time of day; 11.1 mmol/L or above with symptoms suggests diabetes.

interpretation.meaning: Impaired fasting glucose on the World Health Organization definition, a form of prediabetes. NICE flags a fasting level of 5.5 to 6.9 mmol/L as high risk of type 2 diabetes, and US sources start at 5.6, so the lower limit depends on the guideline used
Diabetes if confirmed on a second test, or if symptoms are present

Hypoglycaemia in people with diabetes, usually from insulin or a sulfonylurea; mild episodes are treated with fast-acting carbohydrate as set out in the care plan, and confusion, drowsiness or a seizure is an emergency (call 999)

measures.meaning: Muscle waste cleared by filtration; rises as kidney function falls. Depends on muscle mass.

Estimated glomerular filtration rate in mL/min/1.73 m². A value of 90 or above is normal only if there is no other sign of kidney damage; a value below 60 for three months or more defines chronic kidney disease, and below 15 is kidney failure.
Protein waste; rises with poor kidney function but also dehydration, bleeding into the gut and high protein intake.
Usually reported together; potassium climbs dangerously when kidneys fail.

interpretation.finding: Rising creatinine over hours to days
interpretation.meaning: Acute kidney injury: dehydration, sepsis, obstruction, drugs; usually reversible if caught
Chronic kidney disease, graded from G3a to G5 by the value
Dehydration or gut bleeding rather than kidney damage

kidney-function-tests.limitations: eGFR is an estimate; it is inaccurate at extremes of muscle mass, in pregnancy and in rapidly changing illness. A substantial share of kidney function can be lost before creatinine leaves the normal range.

measures.meaning: The amount of albumin in a single urine sample divided by the creatinine in the same sample. Creatinine leaves the body at a fairly steady rate, so dividing by it corrects for how concentrated or dilute the urine is, which depends on how much the person has drunk. Below 3 mg/mmol is normal to mildly raised (category A1); 3 to 30 is moderately raised (A2); above 30 is severely raised (A3). Combined with eGFR to stage kidney disease, and used to follow how well treatment is protecting the kidneys.

All proteins, not just albumin, used when large amounts leak (above 300 mg/mmol is called the nephrotic range in some NHS laboratory guidance) and when non-albumin proteins are suspected; the ACR is the more sensitive test for the small leaks of early disease.
The old gold standard; a random or early-morning ACR performs as well and is far more convenient, so timed collections are now rarely needed.

A quick bedside screen that detects only larger amounts of protein; it is not sensitive enough to pick up the moderately raised albumin of early kidney damage, so a negative dipstick does not replace a laboratory ACR in people at risk.

urine-protein.limitations: Exercise, fever, infection and standing for long periods raise protein transiently; in the UK an ACR of 3 to 70 mg/mmol is usually confirmed with a repeat early-morning sample, and chronic kidney disease is diagnosed only when the abnormality lasts for more than three months. The ratio shows that the kidney is leaking albumin but not why, so the cause is sought from the history, blood pressure, glucose, blood tests, imaging and sometimes a biopsy. It measures albumin only, so a protein:creatinine ratio is needed when other proteins may be leaking. A dipstick is not a substitute for the laboratory ratio because it misses small leaks. Laboratories in different countries report the ratio in different units, so a result is read against the units and reference information of the laboratory that produced it.

measures.meaning: The stress hormone from the adrenal cortex; highest at 9 am. Low in Addison disease, high in Cushing syndrome. Measured in blood, in a 24-hour urine collection (which averages the day's output and may need repeating because production varies) or in late-night saliva, and often paired with ACTH to work out whether an abnormality arises in the adrenal gland or the pituitary. Severe stress, acute illness and severe depression also raise it.

Sex hormones; measured with LH and FSH from the pituitary to tell gland failure from pituitary failure. In men, testosterone with sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) helps investigate infertility, low libido and erectile dysfunction; prolactin, oestradiol and LH are often measured alongside to see the whole hormonal balance.

Raised by pituitary tumours, stress, many drugs and pregnancy; causes milk production and lost periods. Checked for unexplained milk production, irregular periods, fertility problems and persistent headaches or visual change; in men a raised prolactin often causes a low testosterone, so it is tested when testosterone is found to be low. An underactive thyroid is a common and easily treated cause of a raised prolactin.
Control calcium and bone; a high PTH with high calcium is primary hyperparathyroidism.

The waste product that crystallises in gout; NICE defines hyperuricaemia as a serum urate of 360 micromol/L or more. Its default treatment target in gout is below 360 micromol/L, with below 300 micromol/L suggested for people with tophi, chronic gouty arthritis or ongoing flares; the British Society for Rheumatology recommends below 300 micromol/L for everyone on urate-lowering treatment.

interpretation.meaning: Adrenal insufficiency; confirmed with a synacthen stimulation test. Low sodium and high potassium on the electrolyte panel support the diagnosis of Addison disease

interpretation.finding: Poor cortisol response to Synacthen with high ACTH
interpretation.meaning: Primary adrenal failure (Addison disease), usually with low aldosterone; a poor response can also follow long-standing lack of ACTH from the pituitary, so further tests and endocrine referral separate the two
Makes primary adrenal failure unlikely but does not exclude recent-onset ACTH deficiency from the pituitary, which needs specialist assessment if suspected

interpretation.finding: High cortisol that does not suppress with dexamethasone
interpretation.meaning: Cushing syndrome from a pituitary or adrenal tumour, or from ACTH produced by a tumour elsewhere in the body; severe stress, illness and depression can mimic it, so results are confirmed with repeat and further tests
Primary hyperparathyroidism, usually a single adenoma
Testicular failure; low LH points to the pituitary instead
Macroprolactin (a harmless large form) is excluded, thyroid function and medicines are reviewed, and an MRI of the pituitary is considered
Supports gout, but the level can be normal during an attack, so it is often repeated some weeks after the attack settles

pregnancy-test.what: Detects human chorionic gonadotropin, a hormone that begins to be made in the days after fertilisation, as the embryo implants in the womb. Urine tests give a yes/no answer; a blood test gives a number that normally rises steeply in a healthy early pregnancy. hCG appears in blood and urine within days of the embryo implanting and rises steeply through early pregnancy, which is why home tests become reliable from around the first day of a missed period and some sensitive tests can turn positive a little earlier. The urine test is a widely used point-of-care test: a strip or stick is dipped into urine or held in the stream and shows a line, symbol or word when hCG is present. In hospital, a urine test is done routinely in women of reproductive age with abdominal pain, bleeding or collapse, and before X-rays, operations and certain medicines, because an unrecognised pregnancy, and above all an ectopic pregnancy, changes what happens next.

measures.meaning: Positive from the first day of a missed period; some very sensitive tests can be used earlier. Modern tests detect low levels of hCG. A qualitative result: it says whether hCG is present above the test's detection limit, not how much. First-morning urine is the most concentrated and gives the clearest result when testing early, although most tests work at any time of day once the period is late.

Quantitative; used to track ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage and molar pregnancy, and some tumours. A laboratory blood test can be qualitative (present or absent) or quantitative (the concentration), and serial quantitative results show whether a pregnancy is progressing normally, failing or abnormally sited; results take from a few hours to more than a day.

pregnancy-test.preparation: None; testing before the missed period risks a false negative. If the date of the expected period is unknown, NHS advice is to test at least 21 days (three weeks) after the last unprotected sex. Drinking large volumes beforehand dilutes the urine and can push an early positive below the detection limit.

interpretation.meaning: Pregnant, almost always, provided the instructions were followed; an ultrasound scan at about 6 to 7 weeks can confirm where the pregnancy is

interpretation.finding: Negative urine test with a period still overdue
interpretation.meaning: Possibly tested too early or with dilute urine; repeat after a few days, and seek advice if a second test is negative and the period has still not started

interpretation.finding: Positive test with pain or bleeding
interpretation.meaning: Ectopic pregnancy must be excluded urgently
Failing or ectopic pregnancy

interpretation.finding: Serum hCG unusually high for dates
interpretation.meaning: Twins or a higher multiple, a molar pregnancy or wrong dates; ultrasound clarifies
Resolution of a miscarriage, ectopic or molar pregnancy; followed until it is undetectable

thresholds.context: After the last unprotected sex (three weeks); testing earlier risks a false negative

crp.what: A blood test for C-reactive protein, a protein the liver releases within hours of significant inflammation, infection or tissue injury. It measures the size and course of an inflammatory response and how it changes with treatment, but not its cause. CRP is a general marker: it is often the first laboratory evidence that something inflammatory is happening, with the level rising before pain, fever or other signs are obvious, and its concentration can climb steeply during a severe infection. Because it falls quickly once the trigger settles, repeated measurements are more informative than a single value, and clinicians read it alongside the symptoms, the examination and other tests.

measures.meaning: Starts to rise within hours of a trigger, peaks within a day or two and falls quickly once the trigger resolves. Very high levels suggest bacterial infection or major inflammation; mild elevations are common and non-specific. For adults with a suspected lower respiratory tract infection, NICE uses a point-of-care CRP below 20 mg/L, 20 to 100 mg/L and above 100 mg/L to help decide whether to offer antibiotics. The protein is made by the liver as part of the acute-phase response, so it reflects the whole-body inflammatory signal rather than any one organ. It is also raised after a heart attack, after surgery and in sepsis, and a high-sensitivity version of the assay (hs-CRP) picks up the very low-grade inflammation linked to cardiovascular risk. Laboratories report in different units, so the reference limit printed on the report is the one to use.

interpretation.meaning: Significant bacterial infection or major inflammation until proven otherwise; the source is sought with examination, imaging and cultures

interpretation.finding: Mildly raised CRP (a small rise above the laboratory's reference limit)
interpretation.meaning: Minor inflammation, viral illness, obesity, smoking or recent exertion; interpreted with the clinical picture and often repeated rather than acted on

interpretation.finding: Normal CRP with a high ESR
interpretation.meaning: Consider conditions that raise ESR without much CRP: myeloma, lupus, anaemia, pregnancy
The inflammation is settling or the antibiotic is working; a persistently rising value after surgery prompts a search for infection or a leak

interpretation.finding: Raised CRP in a long-term inflammatory disease
interpretation.meaning: A flare of rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis, lupus or inflammatory bowel disease, or an intercurrent infection; a fall after a change of treatment shows the anti-inflammatory therapy is taking effect

interpretation.finding: Normal CRP very early in an illness
interpretation.meaning: Does not exclude infection, because the level takes hours to rise; a repeat sample the next day is often more informative
